drills.q: Which of the four platforms (LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix, Laminar) can you self-host without an enterprise sales conversation?
drills.a: Langfuse, Phoenix, and Laminar. LangSmith requires an Enterprise contract (reportedly $100K+ minimum) for any self-hosted deployment.

drills.q: Which platform's license is source-available but NOT OSI-approved open source?
Roughly what's the cost gap between LangSmith and Langfuse at 1M trace events/month?
drills.a: LangSmith ~$2,514/mo vs Langfuse ~$101/mo -- over a 20x difference.

drills.q: A procurement policy requires OSI-approved open-source licenses only. Which of the four platforms fails this bar and why, and which two pass cleanly?
drills.a: Phoenix fails -- Elastic License 2.0 is source-available but not OSI-approved. Langfuse (MIT) and Laminar (Apache 2.0) both pass cleanly; LangSmith isn't open source at all.

drills.q: Design an instrumentation strategy today that minimizes lock-in risk regardless of which of these four platforms you pick.
drills.a: Instrument with raw OpenTelemetry using the GenAI semantic conventions rather than a platform-specific SDK/tracer, routed through an OTel Collector so the export destination is a config change. This works cleanly against Phoenix and Laminar; it reduces but doesn't eliminate migration cost off LangSmith/Langfuse since some platform features expect their own SDK shape.

drills.q: Legal flags Langfuse's ClickHouse acquisition as a risk. What's the accurate, non-alarmist answer?
drills.a: Both companies publicly committed to keeping Langfuse MIT-licensed and self-hostable, and ClickHouse has an open-source track record. But license commitments made during acquisition press cycles have a documented pattern of quietly reversing 12-18 months later (MySQL, Redis, Elastic) -- track the LICENSE file and changelog on a recurring cadence rather than treating it as permanently settled.

drills.q: Why does Laminar's ~20x trace compression matter specifically for agent workloads, and what's the catch?
drills.a: Agent runs are chatty (40-75 spans typical, mostly compressible text like prompts/tool args), so compression directly lowers data-volume-based billing for exactly this workload shape. Catch: compression trades some query/analysis latency for storage cost, and the ratio is workload-dependent -- structured/numeric-heavy traces won't compress as well.

drills.q: A team fully committed to LangGraph as their agent runtime is choosing between LangSmith and an OTel-native alternative. Make the case for LangSmith despite its cost/lock-in.
drills.a: LangSmith's node-by-node LangGraph state diffs, 'replay against a new model' regression isolation, and first-party Prompt Hub with zero assembly are genuinely deeper than a generic OTel-native platform offers for that specific stack -- the cost and lock-in is a real tradeoff against real day-one integration depth, not an oversight.

drills.q: A startup with no compliance requirements is choosing an observability platform. What do you pick, and what do you explicitly defer, and why?
drills.a: Pick Langfuse's free cloud tier or Laminar's free self-host tier -- low setup cost, full core features, no enterprise sales cycle. Defer OSI-license-purity concerns and self-hosting infrastructure investment until an actual trigger appears (a customer contract requiring data residency, or cloud pricing starting to bite at volume) -- building for a compliance requirement that doesn't exist yet is premature.

drills.q: Your team picked Phoenix for its OTel-native tracing but now needs a dashboard-and-alert-first tool for 24/7 on-call. Is Phoenix the wrong tool entirely? What's the fix?
drills.a: Not automatically wrong -- its OTel-native tracing and free self-hosting are still real strengths for deep-dive investigation. Since Phoenix is OTel-native, export the same trace data to a dashboard/alerting-first backend in parallel (see T08-classic-obs for alert design), using Phoenix for investigation and the other tool for on-call-facing alerts.

drills.q: Explain why comparing these four platforms on a feature checklist (tracing, evals, prompt management, datasets) is misleading, and what should replace that comparison method.
drills.a: All four now claim near feature parity on a checklist. The real differentiators (license terms, self-hosting cost/accessibility, cost curve shape at 10-100x pilot volume, and how much instrumentation would need rewriting to leave) only surface when you model your actual growth trajectory and constraints against each platform -- build a cost model at projected volume, confirm license/self-host terms against real requirements, and prototype the OTel-portability swap.
